I work with senior people whose English is already good, and almost all of them arrive with the same question. They ask me how to lose the accent. That is not the question. Nobody in an American meeting is scoring your vowels. What they are doing, without knowing it, is following your strong beats. English gives length and height to the words that carry information, and it runs fast and low over everything else, so the listener can find the meaning without effort. When every word arrives with the same weight, nothing is wrong. The grammar is fine, the vocabulary is often better than mine. But the listener now has to sort the sentence himself, and sorting is work. After about a minute of that work, attention goes. People will tell you afterwards that you were hard to follow, and you will think they meant your pronunciation. They did not. They meant they got tired. So here is the first thing I ask for. Break the answer into short groups, three to seven words, and put a real silence at the end of each one. And the second thing. When you need a moment, close your mouth and take it. Do not say um. Silence costs you nothing. A filler costs you credibility, every single time.

Quick note before I forget the day. Two candidates, and the difference had nothing to do with their level of English. The first one, technically, was excellent. Her grammar was close to perfect, better than most native speakers on that panel. But she spoke in one long line, at one speed, with no landing anywhere, and by the fifteen minute mark I had stopped hearing individual sentences. When I read my own notes afterwards I could not tell you what her biggest project was. That is not a language problem. That is a delivery problem, and it cost her the room. The second candidate had a much heavier accent and made two grammar mistakes I noticed. She also did something that I want every candidate to do. I asked her the hardest question of the day, about a program that went badly, and instead of filling the air she stopped. She stayed silent for maybe two seconds, and the whole panel leaned in. Then she gave us three short sentences, each one ending on a full stop you could hear. Everybody in that room remembers her answer. So when you talk to the next group, tell them this from me. Slow down and use the silence. Nobody in the history of this company has ever been rejected for pausing.

First I break the answer into short groups of three to seven words. Then I choose the one word in each group that carries the meaning. I put a small pause at the end of every group. I let my voice fall at the end of every statement. And when I need a second, I pause instead of saying um.
